item.title: Diversity in the teaching of design and arts and crafts must become the standard
item.description: The teaching of design and arts and crafts has evolved significantly in recent years. While the creation of the DNMADE is probably its standard-bearer, the increase in theses and HDRs related to design research, and the development of master’s programmes in several institutions are other significant elements. The evolution of the learning public is also remarkable. Since the creation of the DNMADE, there seems for example to be a significant increase in the relative number of students coming from the general baccalaureate compared to those coming from the ST2A baccalaureate, which is nonetheless dedicated to these studies. We also note the statistically significant and sociologically noticeable increase in “top of the class” students (to borrow the expression of Jean-Laurent Cassely), that is to say, graduates from more traditional fields who undertake further training in an arts and craft profession. It is therefore worthwhile to reflect regularly on these developments and to invite all engaged perspectives to do so.
